Thank you very much, Mr. President, Excellencies. distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. It is an honor to present Estonia's 3rd Voluntary National Review on the Implementation of Sustainable Development Goals. For Estonia, sustainable development is not the new agenda. Already in 1995, we adopted our Sustainable Development Act. In 2005, the Parliament approved a strategy, Sustainable Estonia 21. Today, the Sustainable Development Goals are integrated into Estonia's long-term national strategy, Estonia 2035, and into the sectoral development plans and programs that guide government's action. We also track this progress publicly. Estonia's SDG indicators are available at the Tree of Statistics dashboard. So that our performance is visible not only to the government, but to everyone. Since our previous review in 2020, the world around us has changed dramatically. The COVID-19 pandemic tested our healthcare system, disrupted education, altered supply chains, and exposed vulnerabilities in society. Soon after, Russia launched its full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine. This war has had consequences far beyond Ukraine. It has raised energy and food prices, increased the cost of living, weakened economic stability, and affected progress on poverty, inequality, and economic growth. That is why Estonia's current review pays more attention than before to crisis management and resilience. The lesson is clear: sustainable development cannot be separated from security, democracy, the rule of law, and the ability of societies to withstand shocks. People need to feel that their immediate needs and fears are being addressed. Only thereafter, they can focus on long-term development goals. Overall, Estonia is making solid progress. Fresh data published last week show that Estonia now ranks 12th in the SDG Index. This is a very strong result and places Estonia among the world's leading countries in implementing the Sustainable Development Goals. We see strong results in health and well-being. Health insurance covers more than 95% of the population, and life expectancy is increasing. We continue to perform well in education. Estonia offers high-quality education that is accessible and free of charge, regardless of gender, religion, or socio-economic background. Our education system remains one of the best in the world, and one of the foundations of our resilience. Quality education helps to balance our possible inequalities in our societies. We have also made progress on clean energy. The share of renewables in electricity generation amounted to 68% last year, and renewable energy in final energy consumption has risen by 10 percentage points in 4 years, reaching to 40%. Renewable energy is a rational economic choice, delivering also a cleaner world for everybody. Estonia has also recently adopted its first nuclear energy and safety law, as we expect the first small modular reactor commissioned hopefully around 2035. Digital society remains one of Estonia's strengths. More than 92% of people use the internet. 85% are satisfied with digital public services. And nearly 92% of residents consider Estonia's cybersecurity trustworthy. Estonia continues to advance its digital society through artificial intelligence. With AI Leap program, we are bringing AI into education. Furthermore, we are promoting economy-wide application of AI to boost productivity and support progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals. We attach great importance to the quality of institutions. Estonia ranks joint 12th in the Corruption Perception Index, and 91% of residents consider their neighborhood safe. However, the 3rd place in this year's Press Freedom Index was a step down from last year's 2nd place. Free and independent media is one of the backbones of democracy. Therefore, securing the freedom of press is a priority for Estonia. Our solid progress does not remove responsibility. Several goals require significantly more work. Our focus is on protecting the most vulnerable in our society, including the elderly, people with special needs, and young people. We are not yet on track to achieve our 2035 gender equality goals. The gender gap— gender pay gap has narrowed, and our Gender Equality Index has improved since 2020. But the pace needs acceleration. We continue to reduce our greenhouse gas emissions at a solid pace. Estonia has already reduced emissions by 66% compared to 1990. But our ambition is far higher. Our task is to build an economy that is cleaner, more competitive, and more secure at the same time. For Estonia, the international dimension of sustainable development is equally important. Today, Estonia has become a high-income country with a very high rank in the Human Development Index. This gives us both a moral obligation and a direct interest in contributing to the global well-being. Already from 1997, Estonia became a provider of official development assistance. Development cooperation helps to eradicate poverty, support democratic governance, and strengthen societies. Humanitarian assistance saves lives and supports those affected by natural or man-made disasters, especially the most vulnerable. Ukraine is, and will remain, a top priority for Estonia. Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine is not only a war against one country. It is an attack on the principles that make sustainable development possible: sovereignty, human rights, international law, and the fundamental right of a people to choose their own destiny. That is why Estonia has committed to allocate 0.25% of GDP annually for military and defence assistance to Ukraine in 2024 through 2027. We will also continue to support Ukraine's reconstruction, resilience, and reform efforts, including by co-hosting the 2027 Ukraine Recovery Conference. At the same time, Estonia will continue to respond to the needs of other developing countries, especially the least developed and post-conflict states, small island developing states, and landlocked developing countries. As a small country, we know that our resources are limited, but we also know that our experience in digital governance, cybersecurity, AI, education, transparency, and resilient institutions can be useful to others to bridge the existing development gap. Ladies and gentlemen, the Sustainable Development Goals remain a practical framework for better lives, stronger societies, and a healthier planet. But they will not be achieved by declarations alone. They require implementation, trust, accountability, and cooperation. Estonia remains committed To delivering its part at home, in Europe, with Ukraine, and with our partners across the world. Thank you very much.

In 2025, a new water reservoir was installed, increasing the total water storage capacity to 47 million gallons. Under SDG 7, Affordable and Clean Energy, the Marshall Islands remain committed to ambitious climate action and sustainable energy transition. In 2025, we adopted our Nationally Determined Contribution 3.0, reaffirming our commitment to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 45% below the 2010 levels by 2030 and at least 58% by 2035, with a long-term goal of net-zero emissions by 2050. Their technical assistance, financial contributions, and continued collaborations have been instrumental in helping the RMI advance its sustainable development aspirations.
